It does have some cool new additions like constructing resource gatherers and defences on the map though.  There's a good variety of creature types and map objects, the music is great, the game looks nice, and it seems quite polished with attention to QoL.  The campaign dialogue is pretty funny as well!

And it'd be wise to give it that love, as we have seen few attempts at a HoMM successor that nailed the formula. The engine seems very solid. It's beautiful graphically. I don't have enough time in it to say more about the balance of the title and I'll update my review to reflect the current state of the game as I progress, but for an Early Access title everything needed is there for an incredible framework. 

Currently there are 8 released campaign maps with another 8 planned. My playtime is for just the first, which seems like a hybrid tutorial. Let's hope we see more than those 8, whether it's in the form of DLC or something else because the engine and formula great potential if the developer can nail balance & replayability. Balance will be what determines this games success and I can only comment on the "first level of the campaign." I'll update my review as I venture deeper, but I wanted to throw out early praise and optimism as it broke my heart to see "Mixed" recent reviews for a well-executed Early Access title.

From a gameplay standpoint this stays very close to HoMM but makes some smart refinements:
- instead of a week you have different portions of the day. This is a great concept and allows for differing environmental art and mechanics
- you can invest in mines to increase their production or create garrisons for defending forces
- you can build mini structures in key locations (think caravan nodes / garrisons / watchtowers)
- skills feel more balanced compared to HoMM - eg instead of the worthless eagle eye there is a similar skill that also teaches you a new spell every day (week)
- instead of immediately using things on the battlefield you can collect them (eg think being able to pickup and deliver treasure chests)
- number and power of the hero artifacts you can equip are limited by your hero's mana pool size

They only downsides I've spotted so far:
- the AI doesn't feel very challenging, it feels on par with HoMM2.. though I haven't explored too many maps or difficulties yet so we'll see.
- while the art and sound are gorgeous the animations feel a little interpolated. If I were comparing this to any other game this minor nitpick wouldn't even register but comparing to HoMM2 and 3's phenomenal hand-animations mean that I have to point it out 

It's still early in development, but I think what is here is already very fun and promising - watch out for that "one more turn"

Silence of the Siren is a game that was inspired by HoMM3 but was able to create its own style. The attention to detail is admirable.

Moving on to my criticisms of the game (mostly about UI and visibility),

- Commanders' statistical information can be made visible on the bars on main game screen (or a visibility on/off button can be added to options)

- Mini pop-ups can be added to both battle screens and town screens for quick access to all unit statistics.

- Battle screens feel narrow and cramped and large units block each other's line of sight when stacked on top of each other (This situation becomes inextricable, especially when enemy troops are included in the equation). When I researched how other games have solved this, I noticed that hexagons are kept large in HoMM: Olden Era. A similar solution could be brought to SoTS.

- As in many games of the RTS or TBS genre, choosing a color from the color palette in a multiplayer or singleplayer game can be a solution to the situation I mentioned above as well.

- Friendly fire can be enabled for area-of-effect damage, which can add a tactical layer (the player can be asked in the options whether this will be or not, or it could be depend on the game difficulty).

As a gamer and moviegoer who loves science fiction, it is a really creative idea to bring this theme to this game. If the game feeds itself with the feedback it receives from players during the early access period and follows the roadmap flawlessly, we may be faced with a masterpiece when it goes to full release.

Combat view is basicaly the same, world map movement and strats plays exactly like a HoMM series, the city view design is straight taken from HoMM. Pure perfection.

Some devs were trying - like Songs of Conquest - but for whatever reason they've changed the core flavours of the HoMM, completely ruining it for me. No City view, weird building construction ideas, super gimmicky unit->hero ability activators that backfired big time... and many many more ideas that could be labaled as " I am so smart that I will make new HoMM 3 but better ". I have it on GoG and I never played it again after the launch. Songs of Conquests feels like a mobile game.

Devs who made Heroes of Science and Fiction got it right. They've just copied what is amazing in HoMM, added some flavour and it literaly feels like playing Sci-Fi HoMM.

It always bothered me why studios do not make copies of HOMM3 out of everything. Any IP that has factions, sort of heroes would work. LotR " HoMM ", Witcher " HoMM ", Conan " HoMM ", Dune " HoMM ", Star Trek " HoMM ", Star Wars " HoMM ".
It's unbelievable to me why this is not a thing. Instead we got copycat Moba's, Survival games, Minecraft clones, MMRPG's and Battle Royale cringe. 

For whatever reason one of the most beloved games ever made - which is Heroes of Might and Magic 3 - is not getting copied left and right and I have to wait decades to see one game that comes close.

Thank God that more of that is coming from other studios as well.

Comparison test: 

Songs of Conquest, Silence of the Siren and Pennon and Battle are promising TBS titles in the style of HoMM III/IV. This review aims to highlight their respective strengths and weaknesses. 

Content: 

SoC: Four playable factions. Another three are already planned as DLC. Each race has eight units and one upgrade per unit, as well as a  research tree for economy and warefare, the heroes support exploration and combat with spells. Four story campaigns and a RMG  are available. There is also a map editor. Most maps can be played in single player, co-op or multiplayer in local hot-seat mode or online.  

SotS: Three playable factions - at full release there will be five, each race has units of seven tiers and one upgrade per tier, as well as a war machine, the heroes support exploration and combat with technology (like HoMM III spells)
One branch of the story campaign and nine skirmish maps+nine scenarios are already available.

PaB: Currently campaigns, arena, and online PVP modes are available. There are five factions with distinct features each faction has seven tiers and two upgrades (later apparently three) per tier, as well as a war machine, the heroes support the fight with magic and engage personally. 

World map: 

In all games, the world map is as pretty as it is vividly designed. 

Lavapotion had obviously gone to great lengths to make the world map of SoC as detailed as possible and to pay attention to lovely, pretty details. The world never looks boring here. 

Comparing PaB and SotS:It is clear at first glance that SotS can benefit from a much more detailed graphical representation. PaB, on the other hand, is much clearer and more concise. 

Towns: 

In all three games, buildings are constructed in the towns with resources that are used to recruit troops, defend the base, generate resources, learn spells/techniques and other advantages. In SotS, the buildings are displayed on a town screen. This is missing in PaB.  

In SoC, the city buildings are placed directly on the world map using building site points located near the cities. The interesting feature of SoC's well-designed research system for economic and military purposes is worth highlighting. Among other things, this allows the performance of the troops and economic income to be improved. 

Combat: 

As in HoMM III/IV, combat in all games takes place on a separate combat map, in which the creatures and heroes use their abilities and spells turn by turn to defeat the opposing army. In PaB, as in HoMM IV, the hero is an active figure in the battle and can be attacked by the opposing army. In SotS, the hero uses techniques such as artillery strikes to intervene in the action. Unfortunately, these both games lack the tactical sophistication and brilliance of games like Songs of Conquest, as there are no opportunity attacks or height differences to add tactical depth to the combat. This is a great pity. At least opportunity attacks are part of every tactically demanding game today. Examples include SoC, Spellforce: Conquest of Eo and Age of Wonders Planetfall and IV. I wish that at least opportunity attacks would get implemented in SotS and PaB.

Summary: 

For fans of Heroes of Might and Magic, all three games are definitely worth a closer look. They are beautifully designed, invite you to explore the pretty strategy map and offer an appropriate strategic challenge depending on the level of difficulty. Unfortunately, PaB and SotS lack the tactical depth of Songs of Conquest. 
Silence of the Sirene is a pretty game without any particular weaknesses, but there is still room for improvement in terms of tactical depth. The same applies to Pennon and Battle. PaB's additional flaws are the lack of a town screen and the absurd in-app store, which leaves a less than elegant impression for a PC game.

I've found this game by accident, tried the demo and bought it. Good chance and good decision.

Basically, it uses a tried and tested Heroes III chassis to build upon, ending up (or rather - WILL end up) with something considerably better than everything else that tried to simulate, emulate or downright copy-paste the classic over the years. Even though the game is similar to HoMM in many ways, it's not a clone, it has its own ideas - and they are good ideas too! Even though it's still not finished in terms of content, it's very much playable and enjoyable. 

Why it's not simply a HoMM copy? First of all - it has its own setting, which manages to be both subtly hilarious and well-thought out. That's no sci-fi, it's more like futuristic fantasy (which by the way the HoMM universe also is, although under cover, but let's not get into that now) with dictatorial militaristic moles, zealous cyber-bugs, over-the-top 80's style humans from the future and so on. The dialogue in the campaign is fun to read. Aesthetically, the creatures are interesting to look at, the animations are nice and the map, although cartoonish in general, is quite readable after you get used to it. The balance seems to be all over the place right now, but that's to be expected. Certain creature abilities are quite original. I love the "artillery" type of units. The "spells"... I can't quite figure out how effective they are yet - some of them seem to do quite a good job, others - not so much. As for the heroes - there's a good range of abilities to choose from and so far they all make some sense, but it looks like each hero is just a portrait and a short background - no specialization (at least I couldn't find any) that would make him/her/it unique gameplay-wise. Maybe this is something, which will be implemented later (hopefully).

If you're a potential buyer - at the moment the game has one campaign, some pre-made maps outside of it, 3 playable factions (a fourth one is expected soon, from what I read) and seemingly all, or at least most of its core mechanics in place. From what I've seen, it can easily keep you entertained for at least 40-50 hours with that content alone and that number will raise drastically when other campaigns, factions and so on appear. It's worth it. in short.

One suggestion to the devs (apart from the hero specialization mentioned above) - the concept of building support structures on the map is a nice one, but could use some more flavour. The sentry guns for example can't stop anything but the weakest enemy army - why not add an option to upgrade them? Same with the other types of buildings. Also - it will be nice to have the option to build roads.

All in all, I'm fairly optimistic that the fully baked game will be a worthy Heroes successor, likely surpassing the upcoming new Heroes game from Ubisoft.

[h1] Fellow HoMM 3 Enjoyers, Rejoice! [/h1]

Silence of the Siren (SotS) takes me back to my younger years where I’d spend countless hours playing Heroes of Might and Magic. For fans of the HoMM of old, you’ll feel right at home with SotS – Don’t read further, buy it. If you’ve never played a HoMM game before however, then please do continue reading.

At its core, SotS is a turn-based strategy game featuring three unique factions, and two primary gameplay aspects. The first aspect being exploring the beautifully drawn maps with your commanders (hero). Each day you can travel through the map, collecting various resources or engaging in combat (with neutral enemies or opposing factions) to gain experience and items, among other things.

The second aspect is combat, which occurs on a hexagonal grid with armies at opposing ends, along with a timeline across the bottom displaying unit turn orders. Initially, units appear limited in their combat ability but as you upgrade them, combat becomes much more engaging and rewarding. It’s simple, and just like HoMM, it’s usually a case of whoever has the larger army (or more experienced commander) wins – There’s little in terms of strategy.

Upgrading your units is done through cities, which serves as a hub where you can also hire new commanders and units. Upgrades can be purchased each day (turn) while new units can only be hired once a week (four-turn cycle). Additionally, there’s a day night cycle, which (in addition to new weeks) introduce new gameplay elements, however I thought their impact was miniscule.

If what I’ve written sounds enjoyable, give SotS a try. I highly recommend the game for fans new and old. While the concept may be familiar to most, the game oozes character, delivering a solid entry into the genre.

Overall impressions from gameplay:

This is a really good Heroes experience, the best I had since playing, probably, Heroes V: ToE.  For the ones who want drastic innovations in the genre, this is not the game you are searching for. This is an extremely good recreation of the formula, with a lot of small tweaks sprinkled here and there, so I could like it mechanically better than Heroes V.

Difficulty:

Completed both campaigns on medium, I am very much satisfied: the enemies have been rather forgiving, but not too forgiving for coming to the final battle with two starting armies. In addition, you can always gather bigger army for the final battle, which is both a saving grace and a problem, it is too easy to tweak the difficulty of the final battle of the campaign. Here, I prefer the separate mission with custom army approach of the game like Heroes V, but I see the design choice, and it is more than fine by me.

Map design:

Fine, sometimes entrances to the mines are too far away from the road, I would rotate the objects,

Design overall:

Very good, you are able to see the interactive objects on the map good enough, when you pay attention. Factions are stunning, I immediately fell in love with both UNSS and Fossorians. The Children of the Source also seem very intriguing, and the Sovereign Fleet by now seem fine, I expect the campaign to sell me better on them.

Lore/characters/plot:

Plot is nice and easy, lore captures the attention. Characters are funny, interesting and stand out enough to remember them, I liked character cast from both campaigns, which never happened to me before. 

Map editor: 

Functional, more similar to visual programming approach of something like Heroes III, rather than to scripting approach of Heroes V. Still lacks some cosmetic functions, but overall, by now I am satisfied with the range of possibilities. Looking forward to building my own map, after which I revisit this section.

Silence of the Siren is a shameless [url=https://www.gog.com/en/game/heroes\_of\_might\_and\_magic\_3\_complete\_edition][b]Heroe of Might and Magic 3[/b][/url] clone. In fact Sirens has recently renamed itself to [b]Heroes of Science and Fiction[/b], I guess to make it easier to see the link to the Heroes games at a glance from just the title. There is a reason for this, this game is a clone.

Now being a clone is not a bad thing. [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/867210/Songs\_of\_Conquest/][b]Songs of Conquest[/b][/url], another Heroes-Like game, actually got a lot of hate for being too far from Heroes3 by the Heroes3 Fans. There is a fine line in making a clone. It can't be exactly the same, but it also can't really be that different either. [b]Songs of Conquest[/b] is just too far removed from Heroes3, particularly in the combat, town and magic system, for Heroes3 fans, in all the ways that matter, it is a very different game, but this game..... well it is so overt with being a faithful clone of Heroes3 that it really hits that spot for fans. This is Heroes3, but new.

That is not to say that there are not differences. Despite changing the setting to science fiction from fantasy. While much of the game is nearly identical, there are still a load of significant differences. Curiously, and unlike [b]Songs of Conquest[/b], they never make it not feel like Heroes3.

One of the big differences is that most items can be stored in the hero's inventory. So imagine in Heroes3 you pick up a chest, you then have a choice of taking XP or Gold. In this game you can simply place it in your inventory to open later. Maybe saving them until you trade them to another low level hero. Most items in the game work like this. There are also ways to modify the world map. Mines can be upgraded to increase output. You can build outposts, and other assorted objects like auto turret or a tower (to clear fog of war), there is a fog of war lol. There are a host of cool new buildings like a training ground, a place to do virtual combats without any attrition to your armies. A building to remove a skill, clearing a slot to fill later. There is a host of other cool things as well. Like a "camping" mode where your hero can hold position and slowly gain XP, even if you never activate them. In fact one of the fun little things about the game is finding these small little tweaks to the way Heroes3 plays. An item that allows you to use the same site a second time in one week is a cool example of this.

The unit roster is awesome. As are the neutrals. There are some very new abilities, particularly in the spells, so a new player will need some time to adjust to that, but all in all I think the combat is really fun and satisfying. The GFX look great. I have had a mate say it was a little hard to read the adventure map, but I think that is because the map has the ability to zoom way out. Just zoom into the map a little and I think it is not only very readable, it also looks cool AF.

For the purpose of this review, i am going to assume that you are familiar with the heroes games.
If you are a fan of the heroes series and want to try something similar but still new and with a touch of modern air, this is for you. You will recognise a lot but there are twist to keep it interesting. "creature banks" for example now give you the option between getting a small reward, being able to return again on a new "phase" (basically weeks but only 4turns) or you attack them, getting a bigger reward but disabeling them for a few phases. Recource generators have different upgrade options, making them better overall or giving them defenses.
There is a way stronger element of strategy to the fog of war in this game: instead of having to states: covering the map or being revealed, there are now 3ish. If the fog of war is revealed but no "commander" (heroe) is nearby, there will be a shadow over this area. You will still be able to see the area, its terrain and loot, but if an enemy player were to be there, you would not know. This nicely ties into a brand new mechanic: building. Every commander is now able to build 1 of 4 structures each turn (if you have the recources). These structures range from mining recources, turrets, or outpost to a drone which is able to keep the fog of war at bay so you can always see what is going on there. One last big deviation (albeit welcome) are the outpost and "teleporter" buildings. Every town has a building which allows fast travel between towns and, if you have an outpost build, you can transport one stack of units to this outpost per turn. The "academy" (mage guild) also has a special building which enables you to teach a commander a spell, even if they are far away from the base. Gone are the days of tedious hero chains and backtracking for the sake of magic, these new additions allow for a more relaxed aproach while always keeping a strategic element to it. last but not least: certain units have special abilitys which they can use once per battle, there are active items on the map for commanders to use (regaining movement for example) and a day and night cycle which is not just asthetic but can impact units and co.

Heroes of Science and Fiction is an outstanding game. It shares a lot of similarities with games from the Heroes of Might and Magic series (who'd have thought, right?). It, however, further iterates on the original formula. In my opinion it does so incredibly successfully.

Everything you know and love from its originators is here. The base building, the battles, the overworld, the hero 'magic' system, the unique tiered units which can be upgraded, the various resources. All of it. The main difference is that it's draped in a science fiction theme (yes, really). What stands out to me is the various ways in which you can level your hero. Every level, you can choose which of the three main attributes to upgrade. The options being exploration proficiency, combat power and ability strength. Exploration upgrades provide you with more movement points and increased visibility range on the overworld, combat power strengthens your units' attack and defense in battle and ability power represents the strength of your 'magic' abilities and increases your 'mana' pool.  Additionally, you're provided with a selection of three skills to choose from, which allow you to further specialize your hero. Skills such as War Hawk provide your units with more movement points during battle and a higher initiative rating, while skills like Psyker give you access to Psy Combat abilities, which is a lot like how Geomancer would give you access to earth magic in similar games. All of this grants you a lot of flexibility in how to upgrade and specialize your hero. 

The way in which you can influence your interactions with the overworld is also great. For instance, your heroes can collect and use consumables. These can give you an edge during certain situations. Need to vanquish that enemy hero that's been hitting and running your assets, but he's just out of reach? Use a fuel consumable. Want to cast the reinforce overworld ability, but you're running low on mana?  That recharge cell in your bag might just do the trick. Furthermore, you can place outposts on the overworld, build turrets, lay traps, upgrade resource nodes to provide more of a given resource or allow for the stationing of a garrison. Simply amazing and lovely additions to the formula.

There are currently 5 factions present in the game. Each with their own unique base, heroes and units, that really match their respective faction identities. Upgraded units provide most units with a unique ability, not just a flat stat upgrade. These abilities can really change the tide of battle. For example, a melee unit getting the ability to throw a grenade, which allows you to harass the enemy from afar. 

Upgrades to your base are visible on the overworld, which is a nice little extra that adds to the gameplay experience. I also adore the addition of the teleporter buildings, which allow your heroes to teleport from one base to another for a small gold fee. 

In short, I really like this game. It's a labour of love that's reminiscent of Heroes of Might and Magic 3. Fans of the genre shouldn't hesitate to buy this game, even though it's still in early access. This game is already worth it at full price.

- There are different tech upgrades, but you're "locked in" to only a couple categories. Doesn't make much sense to me.
- If I own something, why do I need a commander next to it to level it up? Doesn't make sense.
- I have yet to find a GREAT reason to use energy. So I don't.
- I have yet to find a GREAT reason to really explore. Exploring the map doesn't really feel rewarding to me. Sure, I get some resources, I get some items, I might even get some artifacts but...meh? 
- The game itself feels, and plays, really slow. Maybe that will change as I get better at the factions and knowing what I'm doing, but this hasn't really GRIPPED me like I wish it did.

For reference, I'm a pretty avid Songs of Conquest player. I know it's unfair to compare the two games, but between these two I definitely have my favorite. Maybe Silence of the Siren (a really weird name choice as it is?) could pick up a few things from SoC and/or vice versa? I dunno. I'm not counting this game out yet, but it's not at a point where I can recommend it. There's no "hook" for me.
